name: Diamin-Azo Blue
lede: Diamin-Azo Blue is a dark, greyed purple-blue from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, a shade close enough to the library's Independence that the two are only a few points apart.

sections.title: A dark plate blue
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 atlas places this swatch at plate XXXV, hue 51″, tone m, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it in block 215 as a grayish violet [1]. In Munsell notation it is 6.7PB 3.3/2.7, a dark, low-chroma blue-violet [1]. Beyond the word diamin, short for diamine, a family of azo dyes used on cotton, what the name itself points to is undocumented in the sources checked here [1].

The nearest color in ColorHub's library is [[independence]], a few points off in grey and hue [1]. Ridgway's plates also carry a near-duplicate he called Dark Anthracene Violet, about two and a half units away, close enough to call the same color under a different name [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this dark blue-violet in 192 of 23,781 paintings, under one per cent [2]. Its single biggest spike is the 1900s, at roughly four times the paintings' overall baseline rate [2]. The earliest match is a 1350 Madonna and Child, centuries before any dye chemistry that could explain the name, so that is a lookalike hue, not a pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is never proof that a particular dye was used [2].
